Minister Bimal Rathnayake yesterday tabled in Parliament a 10-page list of 50 corruption, fraud, and criminal cases involving former Ministers, Rajapaksa family members, senior officials, Police officers, and businesspeople. He rejected claims that the Government was pursuing political revenge.

Rathnayake said the cases were not initiated by the present administration but arose from complaints and legal proceedings dating to the 2015-2019 period. Previous governments had allowed investigations to be suppressed through political influence, he said, whereas investigators now work free of political interference.

Former Ministers on the list include Johnston Fernando, Wimal Weerawansa, Mahindananda Aluthgamage, Basil Rajapaksa, Rajitha Senaratne, Ravi Karunanayake, Prasanna Ranatunga, A.H.M. Fowzie, Bandula Gunawardana, and Rohitha Bogollagama. Rajapaksa family members named are Namal, Yoshitha, Gotabaya, Shiranthi, Rohitha, Chamal, and Shashindra Rajapaksa.

The largest sum cited relates to Nissanka Senadhipathi, over alleged unlawful possession of firearms through a private security company and losses reportedly of Rs. 11.4 billion. Basil Rajapaksa faces allegations over the spending of Rs. 3 billion in Divi Neguma funds on roofing sheets during an election period; he was acquitted by the High Court, and the Attorney General has appealed. Former Presidential Secretary Lalith Weeratunga’s case concerns the use of Rs. 600 million in Telecommunications Regulatory Commission funds to distribute sil cloth during the 2014 Presidential Election. It has resulted in a conviction now under appeal.

The list also covers the Central Bank Bond transactions, involving former Central Bank of Sri Lanka Governor Arjuna Mahendran and businessman Arjun Aloysius. Other cases include Namal Rajapaksa’s alleged receipt of Rs. 70 million from India’s Krrish Group, alleged fraud exceeding $ 7 million in the MiG-27 aircraft procurement, and Rs. 234 million allegedly used to set up the Carlton Sports Network.

It further includes proceedings over the 2019 Easter Sunday attacks, the killings of Lasantha Wickrematunge and Wasim Thajudeen, the disappearance of Prageeth Eknaligoda, and the attacks on journalists Keith Noyahr and Upali Tennakoon.

title: Govt. launches national initiative to establish  Sri Lanka’s first National Building Code | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 9 October 2026 00:00
-     - 54

Defence Secretary Air Vice Marshal (Retd.) 

Sampath Thuyacontha

The Defence Ministry and National Building Research Institute (NBRI) have initiated a landmark national initiative to formulate and establish the first-ever National Building Code of Sri Lanka (NBCSL), marking a significant step towards strengthening the safety, quality, sustainability, and disaster resilience of buildings across the country.

Defence Secretary Air Vice Marshal (Retd.) Sampath Thuyacontha chaired this meeting at the Defence Ministry yesterday in this regard, with the participation of senior officials of line institutes, including the NBRI, National Planning Department (NPD), Urban Development Authority (UDA), and Construction Industry Development Authority (CIDA).

The project proposal submitted by the NBRI to the NPD has been approved for the implementation of the project during 2026-2028 and followed by the Cabinet approval granted on 21 October 2025 (Ref. 25/1928/803/054) based on a Memorandum submitted by the President and Defence Minister. The implementation of the project is jointly managing by the NBRI, CIDA, and UDA with the consultation of all relevant stakeholders.

Sri Lanka currently does not have a single, legally established National Building Code. Building design and construction practices rely on a combination of international standards, including the International Building Code (IBC), Eurocodes, British Standards, and Indian Standards, together with various local regulations and sector-specific requirements. While these standards provide valuable technical guidance, their selective and sometimes combined applications may result in inconsistencies in design verification, approval, and enforcement.

The need for a nationally applicable code is particularly important given Sri Lanka’s exposure to floods, landslides, high winds, and other natural hazards, as well as its diverse climatic, geological, and environmental conditions. A code tailored to these national circumstances will provide a clear and consistent basis for safer design, construction, maintenance, and regulatory oversight.

The proposed NBCSL will establish a coherent national framework aligned with internationally recognised best practices while adapting requirements to Sri Lanka’s local conditions. It will address ten key technical areas, including structural safety, fire safety, sustainability, and universal accessibility, together with practical mechanisms for permitting, inspection, compliance, and enforcement.

The initiative has two complementary objectives: to consolidate Sri Lanka’s fragmented building regulatory environment into a unified national framework; and to establish the institutional and implementation mechanisms required for its consistent application nationwide. This will include clearly defined institutional responsibilities, approval and permitting procedures, inspection and enforcement arrangements, and capacity building for regulators and construction industry professionals.

The formulation process will be supported by extensive consultation with Government institutions, professional bodies, academia, the construction industry, and the public, ensuring that the Code is technically robust, nationally relevant, and practical to implement.

A qualified consulting firm will be selected through a competitive procurement process in accordance with National Procurement Agency Guidelines. The assignment is expected to be implemented over 24 months, culminating in the preparation and gazetting of the NBCSL. The initiative will be financed through the Consolidated Fund. 

“This initiative reflects the Government’s firm commitment to protecting lives and property through modern, science-based construction standards. A National Building Code is long overdue, and its development marks a significant step towards a safer and more resilient Sri Lanka.” 

The Defence Ministry and the NBRI has called for Expressions of Interest (EOIs) from qualified consultancy firms to undertake this nationally significant assignment.

title: Dedicated 12 years to Sri Lanka’s street dogs British Vet to run 620 km across the island | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 9 October 2026 00:04
-     - 28

A veterinary surgeon who has dedicated almost 12 years of her life to caring for Sri Lanka’s street dogs is preparing to run 620 km across the island in one of the biggest challenges of her life.

Dr. Janey Lowes, founder of WECare Worldwide, will set off from Point Pedro on today (9), running from the northernmost tip of Sri Lanka to Dondra in the south. Her 22-day challenge, called ‘The Dog Jog’, will take her through communities across the country, including Anuradhapura, Kandy and Horton Plains, as she attempts to raise $ 2 million towards a new veterinary hospital, rehabilitation centre and veterinary training facility.

The distance is equivalent to almost 15 marathons, with Dr. Lowes covering more than a half marathon every day through Sri Lanka’s heat, humidity, hills and tropical weather. But behind the physical challenge lies a much bigger ambition: to create a lasting veterinary legacy for Sri Lanka.

Dr. Lowes first came to Sri Lanka in 2014 and was struck by the number of street dogs living without access to veterinary treatment.

She returned months later and founded WECare Worldwide. What was originally intended to be a one-year project became her life’s work.

Today WECare provides free veterinary treatment to street dogs, runs community neutering and vaccination programmes and supports veterinary education and training.

Dr. Lowes said: “For almost 12 years, Sri Lanka has been my home and its street dogs have been my life. “I’ve seen incredible kindness towards community dogs here, but I’ve also seen animals suffering from injuries and illnesses simply because the veterinary resources aren’t available where they’re needed.

“Our team works incredibly hard, but our current hospital is constantly at capacity.

“The Dog Jog is about creating something much bigger and longer-lasting. We want to build facilities that allow us to treat thousands more animals, but we also want to share skills and knowledge with veterinary professionals across Sri Lanka.

“If we can strengthen veterinary care across the country, the impact can reach dogs in communities far beyond the area we can physically cover ourselves.”

A $ 2 million ambition for Sri Lanka

WECare estimates that around three million dogs live on Sri Lanka’s streets. The charity currently operates from southern Sri Lanka, providing emergency treatment and taking veterinary services into local communities through its Catch-Neuter-Vaccinate-Release program. Since WECare was established in 2014, the charity says it has carried out tens of thousands of rabies vaccinations and neutering procedures and treated thousands of sick and injured animals.

The proposed new development will include a purpose-built veterinary hospital, dedicated rehabilitation centre and veterinary training centre.

The two clinical facilities are expected to allow WECare to help around 3,000 additional animals every year.

The training centre could have an even wider impact.

WECare plans to provide practical training for veterinary surgeons, workshops and continuing professional development, with the aim of up-skilling over 200 veterinary professionals each year.

The charity also hopes to help develop Sri Lanka’s first nationally recognised veterinary nursing qualification.

Dr. Lowes added: “This project isn’t only about the dogs that come through WECare’s doors.

“We receive reports about sick and injured dogs from communities across Sri Lanka that we simply don’t have the resources to reach.

“By sharing knowledge and practical skills with the wider veterinary community, we can help create an impact far beyond our own hospital.

“This country has given me so much. I want the Dog Jog to help create something that belongs to Sri Lanka and benefits its animals, veterinary professionals and communities for years to come.”

Running the length of Sri Lanka

‘The Dog Jog’ begins at Point Pedro on 9 October 2026 and is scheduled to finish at Dondra 22 days later. Along the way, Dr. Lowes and the WECare team hope Sri Lankan communities, dog lovers, veterinary professionals and supporters will follow the challenge, meet the team along the route and help spread the message.

Dr. Lowes admits she is far from a natural endurance runner.

“I hadn’t run since school before I started training for this,” she said.

“Training while working full-time as a vet in Sri Lanka has been tough. There have been days when I’ve wondered what on earth I’m doing.

“But every day at the hospital we meet dogs that have survived extraordinary injuries and suffering.

“When I think about what they go through, running 620 km suddenly feels like something I have to try.

“I’m suffering so that street dogs don’t have to.”

title: Historic Lithuanian visit marks new chapter in Sri Lanka-Lithuania relations | Daily FT

Lithuania and Sri Lanka have taken an important step towards closer bilateral relations following a three day official visit by Lithuania’s Foreign Affairs Vice-Minister Vidmantas Verbickas. Held as the two countries celebrate 30 years of diplomatic relations, the visit combined their first formal political consultations with discussions on digital transformation, academic engagement and economic cooperation.

The Vice-Minister visited Sri Lanka from 4 to 6 October at the invitation of Foreign Affairs Deputy Minister Arun Hemachandra. Ambassador of Lithuania to Sri Lanka Diana Mickevieiene joined the engagements alongside the Lithuanian delegation, which departed Sri Lanka on 7 October.

The central diplomatic engagement was the inaugural political consultations at Sri Lanka’s Foreign Affairs, Foreign Employment and Tourism Ministry, co-chaired by Vice-Minister Verbickas and Deputy Minister Hemachandra. Discussions covered bilateral political relations, domestic and regional developments, trade and investment, tourism, and cooperation in multilateral forums, including the United Nations and candidatures.

The signing of a Memorandum of Understanding on political consultations gave these exchanges a framework for continued engagement. Regular consultations will allow the two countries to review their relationship, follow up on shared priorities and address matters of mutual interest through direct dialogue.

For Sri Lanka, the mechanism offers a means of deepening ties with Lithuania, a European Union member, while developing partnerships in areas where the two countries have complementary interests. Its significance lies in creating continuity, allowing the discussions held during the visit to become part of a sustained diplomatic process.

Foreign Secretary Aruni Ranaraja, together with the heads and senior officials of the Ministry, extended their fullest support to making the visit successful and fruitful. Their guidance and coordination, alongside the work of the Protocol Division, helped facilitate the meetings and the wider official program.

Digital cooperation emerged as a substantial area of common interest. In discussions with Digital Economy Deputy Minister Eng. Eranga Weeraratne, the delegation explored cooperation in digitalisation, GovTech, digital public services and artificial intelligence. Lithuania expressed its readiness to share experience in developing secure, innovative and people centred digital solutions.

The delegation’s visit to GovTech Sri Lanka and meeting with the Sri Lanka Association for Software and Services Companies (SLASSCOM) connected this dialogue with institutions and businesses involved in Sri Lanka’s digital development. Discussions addressed digital infrastructure, financial technology, information and communication technology, innovation, effective public services and the growth of technology businesses.

Lithuania’s experience in digital government and its growing FinTech sector offer a basis for practical cooperation. The meetings provided an opportunity to exchange experiences and explore how expertise, institutional links and business partnerships could support Sri Lanka’s digital economy.

Academic engagement was another important part of the program. At the University of Colombo, Vice-Minister Verbickas met Vice Chancellor Prof. Indika Mahesh Karunathilake and delivered a lecture on Lithuania’s foreign and security policy in a changing geopolitical context.

Students, faculty, experts and journalists participated in the exchange, gaining insight into Lithuania’s perspective on the evolving international security environment. The engagement strengthened direct contact with Sri Lanka’s academic community and encouraged a wider understanding of the two countries’ interests and experiences.

Closer academic relations could create new pathways for Sri Lankan students, researchers and professionals to connect with Lithuanian universities, research institutions and industries. Academic exchanges, joint research, postgraduate education and professional training are 

promising areas for future collaboration. Developing these opportunities will require continued engagement between the relevant institutions, building on the contacts established during the visit.

The delegation also met representatives of the European Union in Colombo and visited the Honorary Consulate of Lithuania, where Honorary Consul R.M. Manivannan warmly hosted the visitors. Discussions considered the Consulate’s contribution to bilateral relations and opportunities to strengthen trade, technology, business and institutional cooperation.

The delegation expressed appreciation for the Honorary Consul’s support and for the continued commitment of Kanchana Kodituwakku and the Consulate team to strengthening friendship and ties between the people of both countries.

Beyond the official meetings, the visit reflected the personal and cultural connections that sustain the relationship. In Ahangama, a gathering hosted by Vilma Mockuviene brought the delegation together with Lithuanian nationals residing in Sri Lanka. It offered an opportunity to hear about their experiences and recognise their contribution to friendship and cultural understanding. Visits to historic Galle Fort and Gangaramaya Temple also introduced the delegation to aspects of Sri Lanka’s heritage.

The anniversary was celebrated through a special concert co organised by the Embassy of Lithuania, Alliance Française de Colombo and the Honorary Consulate. Lithuanian pianist Aleksandra Kolpakovaite-Dharmawardhane and Sri Lankan violinist Shehani Fernando performed works by composers from both countries, including Lithuania’s celebrated composer and artist Mikalojus Konstantinas  iurlionis.

Vice-Minister Verbickas and Foreign Secretary Aruni Ranaraja addressed the gathering, highlighting the role of cultural exchange in strengthening bilateral relations. A reception hosted by the Honorary Consul brought together government representatives, diplomats, business leaders and other distinguished guests to mark the anniversary and continue discussions in an informal setting.

The Embassy of Lithuania to Sri Lanka, under the leadership of Ambassador Diana Mickevieiene, and Honorary Consul R. M. Manivannan extended their fullest support to the mission. Their coordination with the Consulate team and Sri Lankan partner institutions contributed to a 

program that brought diplomatic discussions together with technological, academic, cultural and community engagement.

Thirty years after the establishment of diplomatic relations, the visit demonstrated the scope for a more active partnership between Lithuania and Sri Lanka. The political consultation mechanism provides a lasting diplomatic foundation, while the digital and academic exchanges offer areas in which both countries can pursue practical results. Continued engagement will be central to turning these opportunities into benefits for institutions, businesses and people in both countries.

The Sri Lanka Tourism Development Authority (SLTDA) helps investors by providing information and guidance on legal and regulatory requirements and by coordinating with the relevant state agencies, he said. It also works with industry stakeholders to make tourism service providers aware of the standards needed to establish, register and operate an enterprise, and it offers them technical support.

Under the Clean Sri Lanka program, the Presidential Secretariat has met tourism sector entities and state agencies on grading accommodation and amenities. So far, 10 tourism facility centres have been identified.

The Deputy Minister said the National Tourism Policy includes environmental measures under its second main policy theme. It proposes assessing the carrying capacity of ecologically sensitive areas, meaning the number of visitors a site can absorb without lasting damage, and introducing environmental controls. New tourism infrastructure must meet sustainability standards, including the use of renewable energy, proper waste and wastewater management, and minimising or eliminating single-use plastics.

On skills, Prof. Ranasinghe said the Sri Lanka Institute of Tourism and Hotel Management (SLITHM) runs nine hotel schools, one in each province. Together they send more than 6,000 trained young men and women into the hospitality and tourism sectors each year.

Jiffry Mohamed, a Director of A Y Investments Impex Ltd., of ‘Supernova Complex’, Bankshall Street, Colombo, was produced in the Negombo Magistrate’s Court on allegations of receiving deposits of money from the bank account of the 1st suspect, one Fernando. President’s Counsel M. M. Zuhair, appearing with Sanjay Perera, M. D. C. Jayamini and Mayurika de Silva for Jiffry Mohamed, filed written submissions stating that Jiffry Mohamed is a businessman of repute with no previous convictions or involvement with the police or courts. His business accounts are open for deposits, into which he regularly receives advance payments from multiple importers for the import of goods. He is a service provider and deposits the payments received in banks. Thereafter, it is the bank which converts the rupees into foreign currencies and transfers the money to the foreign exporters of goods to Sri Lanka. This is a lawful process under the Import and Export Control Act Regulation No 1 of 2011.

Counsel submitted that, according to the police, Jiffry Mohamed had received over Rs. 74 billion into his rupee accounts during the years 2024 and 2025. The Negombo Magistrate, following the written submissions filed on behalf of the 4th suspect, directed the Negombo Headquarters Police to file a detailed report on the evidence relating to the allegations. title: Sri Lanka urged to build digital trade chapters into trade deals | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 9 October 2026 00:00
-     - 32

From left: SLASSCOM Executive Director Chaminda de Silva, ODI Global International Economic Development Group Director Prof. Dirk Willem te Velde, Digital Economy Deputy Minister Eng. Eranga Weeraratne, President’s Chief Advisor on Digital Economy and GovTech Sri Lanka Chairman Dr. Hans Wijayasuriya and ODI Global Visiting Senior Fellow Dr. Ganeshan Wignaraja at the launch of the report

Sri Lanka should negotiate comprehensive digital trade chapters in all future trade agreements, covering both goods and services, to remove barriers to cross-border e-commerce. 

The recommendation comes from an ODI Global report launched in Colombo yesterday.

The chapters would set clear, enforceable rules on data flows, electronic transactions and digital market access, said the report, “E-commerce and international trade in Sri Lanka: Findings from a survey of 953 exporters and importers”. It was prepared in collaboration with the Sri Lanka Association for Software and Services Companies (SLASSCOM) and GovTech Sri Lanka.

Ongoing and future negotiations with India, China, Thailand, the UK and the European Union could include provisions on paperless trade, e-signatures and cross-border data flows with safeguards, the report said. They could also include a ban on customs duties on electronic transmissions and de minimis thresholds, the values below which low-value shipments are exempt from duties and taxes. The report said these could be complemented by standalone digital economy agreements, such as one modelled on the UK-Singapore Digital Economy Agreement, and by targeted cooperation on fintech, payments and cybersecurity.

The researchers also recommended that Sri Lanka actively pursue accession to the Digital Economy Partnership Agreement (DEPA). DEPA is currently implemented by Chile, New Zealand and Singapore and is open to new members. Its modular structure offers a practical way to align with global standards on digital trade, interoperability and data governance, while gaining technical assistance, the report said.

Beyond DEPA, the report recommended that Sri Lanka seek observer or dialogue partner status in the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement and engage with the WTO Joint Statement Initiative on E-Commerce, both of which are shaping the rules of global digital trade. Early participation would give Sri Lanka a seat at the table, influence over rules that directly affect its exporters, and access to the technical support needed for reforms at home, it said.

The trade policy push rests on evidence that e-commerce is already widening Sri Lanka’s export reach. The survey of 953 trading firms, conducted between October 2025 and February 2026, found that 70% of exporters and 75% of importers use e-commerce. Adoption is highest among micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs), at 72%, against 56% among large exporters.

The report said e-commerce could act as a ‘magic bullet’ for exports by opening up whole regions rather than single markets. Among exporters using e-commerce, 61% sell to the Middle East and 61% to Europe, against 48% and 41% of traditional exporters. Some 47% export groceries and packaged foods, which are hard to ship through traditional channels, against 14% of non-users. Traditional exporters, by contrast, rely more on large single markets such as the US, China and the UK.

The Government responded at the launch. “E-commerce presents Sri Lankan businesses, particularly MSMEs, with a significant opportunity to reach global markets. Our priority must be to create an enabling environment by simplifying trade processes, strengthening digital infrastructure and logistics, and building the skills needed to compete globally,” Digital Economy Deputy Minister Eng. Eranga Weeraratne said.

The Government targets growth in the digital economy from $ 3.5-4 billion to $ 15 billion by 2030, supported by a $ 50 million World Bank loan.

“Building a globally competitive digital economy requires a clear understanding of where we stand and where we need to go. Rigorous, firm-level research such as this provides essential evidence for benchmarking our progress, understanding businesses’ first-hand experiences, and shaping the policies and interventions that will advance Sri Lanka’s competitiveness in digital trade,” President’s Chief Advisor on Digital Economy and GovTech Sri Lanka Chairman Dr. Hans Wijayasuriya said.

At home, the report calls for a targeted, outcome-oriented National E-Commerce Policy, drawing on practice in Malaysia, Singapore and the United Arab Emirates. The policy would set measurable national targets for e-commerce growth and digital trade participation. It would also define minimum standards for internet, payments and logistics infrastructure and create a whole-of-Government coordination mechanism with strong public-private engagement. Alongside it, the report recommends a legal and regulatory framework for cross-border e-commerce that clearly distinguishes business-to-consumer from business-to-business trade and ensures a level playing field between domestic and international players.

The report was launched at GovTech Sri Lanka at an event jointly organised by ODI Global and SLASSCOM. Speakers included ODI Global International Economic Development Group Director Prof. Dirk Willem te Velde. ODI Global Visiting Senior Fellow Dr. Ganeshan Wignaraja and report co-author Anishka De Zylva presented the findings, followed by a moderated discussion on the reforms needed to help Sri Lankan firms succeed online.

title: Rabies-free Sri Lanka: One health and vital role of veterinarians | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 9 October 2026 00:26
-     - 22

Rabies remains one of the world’s deadliest yet most preventable diseases. As a zoonotic disease transmitted mainly through infected animals, preventing human deaths ultimately depends on controlling the disease at its source. While Sri Lanka has made remarkable progress in reducing rabies over the years, achieving the goal of a rabies-free nation will require a renewed commitment to the One Health approach and greater recognition of the leadership role veterinarians can play in rabies prevention.

As a veterinarian and a virologist who has spent much of my professional career studying infectious diseases affecting both animals and humans, I have come to appreciate that rabies is one of the clearest examples of why human and animal health cannot be separated. A patient presenting to a hospital following exposure to rabies is often the final link in a chain of events that began much earlier in an infected animal. Breaking that chain before human exposure occurs is the most effective way to save lives.

Physicians play an indispensable role in treating bite victims, administering post-exposure prophylaxis, and preventing fatalities. Their contribution to rabies control is both essential and admirable. However, rabies prevention begins long before a patient reaches a hospital. The primary tools for eliminating rabies are mass animal vaccination, disease surveillance, responsible pet ownership, public education, and effective dog population management, all areas in which veterinarians possess specialised training and expertise.

The One Health concept recognises that human, animal, and environmental health are closely interconnected. Rabies illustrates this principle better than almost any other disease. No single profession, ministry, or institution can eliminate rabies alone. Success requires close collaboration among veterinarians, medical professionals, public health authorities, local government bodies, animal welfare organisations, educational institutions, community groups, and the private sector.

As veterinarians, we contribute to rabies control by preventing the disease before it reaches people. Through vaccination programs, disease surveillance, public education, responsible pet ownership, dog sterilisation initiatives, and humane animal population management, we help break the cycle of transmission at its source. Every dog successfully vaccinated represents not merely an animal protected, but potentially several human lives safeguarded from a disease that is almost always fatal once clinical signs develop.

Recognising and strengthening veterinary leadership in rabies prevention should not be viewed as diminishing the role of the medical profession. Rather, it ensures that each profession contributes its unique expertise within a coordinated national strategy. Doctors save lives through treatment. Veterinarians save lives through prevention. Both are indispensable to a successful rabies elimination program.

A truly effective One Health strategy requires strengthening cooperation among all stakeholders and better utilisation of available resources by emphasising prevention. Investing in vaccination, surveillance, community awareness, responsible animal ownership, sterilisation programs, and humane dog population management is not only more cost-effective but also more humane than relying mainly on post-exposure treatment after bites. This approach will also enhance disease surveillance, data sharing, outbreak response, and public awareness across sectors, creating a more resilient public health system.

Sri Lanka has already demonstrated that rabies can be controlled. The challenge now is to eliminate it. To achieve this goal, we must continue investing in veterinary public health services, strengthen cooperation between the animal and human health sectors, and fully embrace the One Health philosophy. The surest way to prevent human rabies deaths is to stop the disease where it originates: in animal populations.

A rabies-free Sri Lanka is an achievable goal. It will be reached most effectively when veterinarians, doctors, public health authorities, local governments, animal welfare groups, civil society organisations, academia, and the private sector work together under the banner of One Health, united by a common commitment to protecting both human and animal lives.

Prevention is not only better than cure; in the case of rabies, it is the key to elimination. By empowering veterinarians to lead prevention efforts and fostering collaboration across all sectors, Sri Lanka can become a regional model for One Health-based rabies control.

(The author is Professor of Virology, Robert & Julia Simmons Endowed Professor of Infectious Diseases, School of Veterinary Medicine, Louisiana State University, USA. The views expressed are personal and do not necessarily reflect those of Louisiana State University)

title: Independence of Independent Director,  a key differentiator in Board effectiveness | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 9 October 2026 00:24
-     - 83

On paper, corporate governance in Sri Lanka is a picture of statutory precision. Open the annual report of nearly any listed enterprise on the Colombo Stock Exchange, and you will find a neatly arranged matrix certifying Board compliance. Checkmarks confirm that Directors meet every criterion required by the Securities and Exchange Commission, local listing rules, and corporate governance codes. No former executive ties, no material pecuniary transactions, no family relations among promoters, and strict adherence to tenure limits. Mathematically and legally, the Board is independent. Yet inside the Boardroom, when the doors close and strategic or ethical fault lines emerge, this structural compliance is just an illusion.

The fundamental crisis of corporate governance today is not a failure of regulatory definition, but a confusion of identity. We have mistaken statutory independence for independence of thought. Regulators have spent decades perfecting an objective, check-the-box framework designed to filter out mechanical conflicts of interest. In doing so, they solved the quantifiable parameters of independence while leaving its most critical, unquantifiable dimension entirely unguarded. A Director can easily pass every legal test imposed by securities regulators, meeting every letter of the law, while remaining bereft of an individual opinion and being beholden to the largesse of the person or organisation in control.

Independence of thought cannot be codified into a negative checklist. It is a psychological posture, a willingness to invite cognitive friction, and an intellectual courage to break consensus. Modern Board nomination processes, however, give scant recognition to these qualities. Directors continue to be sourced through shared social and school networks, executive recruitment ecosystems, and implicit cultural alignments. The result is a subtle, self-reinforcing corporate conformity. The candidate arrives at the Board table legally pristine yet psychologically bound to the very management or controlling shareholders they were appointed to oversee.

Quiet crisis

This dynamic yields a dangerous phenomenon: the “blind” rubber stamp. When charismatic founders or overbearing CEOs push aggressive accounting, questionable related-party transactions, or flawed strategic pivots, paper-independent Directors rarely mount an active defense. Their silence is not born of overt corruption, but of structural groupthink, deference to authority, and the unspoken pressure to remain a “collegial” team player; a prerequisite for retaining lucrative Board seats and prestige.


The recruitment and election of independent Directors reveal a quiet crisis in corporate governance. There is a fundamental mismatch between what Boards require and what candidates seek. In candidate pools in Sri Lanka, a disproportionate number of applicants view independent directorships not as a rigorous civic duty, but as a prestigious supplement to their retirement income. Retirement pocket money! For many semi-retired executives, a Board seat offers the ideal soft landing after decades in the corporate pressure cooker. It provides high-margin fees, executive perks, and elevated social status in exchange for quarterly attendance and polite consensus. Yet effective directorship demands precisely the opposite posture: active intellectual curiosity, continuous engagement, and a fearless willingness to challenge executive leadership and control shareholders. When candidates pursue directorships primarily as passive revenue streams, Boardrooms lose their vital tension, transforming critical oversight into comfortable, rubber-stamping routine.

This dynamic corrupts the fiduciary relationship from within. Directors who rely on Board stipends to finance their retirement quickly develop a strong incentive to preserve the status quo. Fearful of jeopardising their renewal, they hesitate to ask uncomfortable questions, scrutinise management projections, or resist reckless corporate strategy. They absorb pre-packaged Boardroom decks uncritically, exhibiting polite compliance as responsible leadership. The result is a governance structure that looks robust on paper while remaining hollow in practice. When major corporate collapses occur, stakeholders and regulators express shock that an audit committee composed entirely of qualified, independent Directors failed to spot or stop obvious red flags. But the failure was predictable. 

An independent Director who lacks independence of mind is merely a bystander with a legally certified mandate. If corporate governance is to serve its true purpose, i.e., protecting minority shareholders, ensuring systemic accountability, and safeguarding market integrity, we must confront an uncomfortable truth. Regulatory compliance on paper is no substitute for moral independence in practice. Until the market moves beyond legalistic definitions and begins evaluating Boards on intellectual courage, critical inquiry, and true freedom of thought, the independent Director will remain corporate governance’s most expensive placebo.

Regulatory definitions operate primarily on negative proof. If a candidate has no explicit commercial transactions with the firm, regulatory bodies deem them independent. However, compliance with formal criteria guarantees neither critical distance nor ethical fortitude. Structural independence routinely fails to account for subtle, insidious pressures that dilute Board oversight. Directors often share social networks, elite club memberships, executive backgrounds, and “old school ties” with the CEO or key shareholders. 


These shared socio-economic backgrounds foster unspoken peer pressure, consensus bias, and a strong reluctance to disrupt Boardroom collegiality. Furthermore, even in the absence of financial motivation, Directors frequently develop implicit loyalty to the CEO who sponsored their nomination. The desire to remain in good standing, secure re-nomination, or preserve social harmony continuously undermines objective scrutiny. 

Modern corporate history is filled with governance failures where Boards met every legal requirement for Director independence on paper, yet failed to challenge flawed strategies, opaque accounting, or imperial leadership. Formal codes measure a Director’s legal status, but governance outcomes depend entirely on a Director’s actual behavior. The former can be codified; the latter can only be evaluated through historical conduct.

Evolution of Boards

The evolution of corporate Boards from investor-driven watchdog committees into modern governing bodies reflects a fundamental shift in how business value and accountability are defined. Historically, Board composition leaned heavily toward insider executives, founding families, and dominant capital contributors whose sole objective was maximising short-term equity returns. However, the modern marketplace, marked by the shift from shareholder primacy to stakeholder capitalism, demands a broader fiduciary mandate. Today, Boards must balance financial performance with the interests of employees, customers, local communities, and regulatory bodies. This transition, combined with the proliferation of Public Limited Companies (PLCs) featuring widely dispersed minority shareholders, has made the call for truly independent Directors louder and more urgent than ever before.

In recent times, a primary driver for independent oversight is the protection of minority shareholders against the self-serving actions of a controlling bloc. In many dispersed-ownership structures, majority owners or founding executives can extract private benefits through non-market related-party transactions, executive compensation schemes, or strategic choices that favor insider entities over public equity holders. Independent Directors, unbound by personal, financial, or familial ties to management, act as crucial fiduciaries who ensure that corporate decisions treat all capital providers equitably. 

For instance, during the 2009 Satyam scandal in India, controlling founders attempted to divert over $ 1.5 billion into affiliated family business entities. Strong opposition from independent voices on the Board and retail investors blocked the transaction, illustrating how crucial independent oversight is for preserving minority equity value. Regulatory interventions following high-profile corporate failures have also accelerated this movement. Disasters like Enron in 2001 and Volkswagen’s “Dieselgate” in 2015 highlighted the systemic risks of insular, compliant Boards that foster groupthink and ignore compliance failures. In response,
frameworks like the Sarbanes-Oxley Act in the United States and global stewardship codes mandated that key committees, such as audit, nomination, and remuneration, be led by independent Board members to restore public trust.

The evolution of corporate governance is an example of irony. Boards of Directors were initially created for one sacred, noble purpose: to keep wild, empire-building CEOs from burning through investor cash on private jets and gold-plated vanity projects. Today, the joke is on the founders. Instead of reining in rogue executives, Boards now spend their days acting as overpaid babysitters in a ruthless game of shareholder feudalism. Their primary crusade? Protecting defenseless minority investors and innocent stakeholders from the predatory whims of the very controlling shareholders who appointed them in the first place. It is an absolute masterpiece of institutional irony. The Board, hired as the CEO’s watchdog, is muzzling the majority owners who bought the leash. Corporate democracy at its absolute finest, where the referee is paid by the tyrant to protect the peasants from the tyrant!

I have experienced firsthand that truly independent Directors unlock significant hidden value by transforming Board dynamics and expanding organisational capacity. Free from internal political pressure, independent Directors provide objective strategic pressure-testing on capital allocation, M&A, and major strategic pivots. Their external perspective enables early risk detection, spotting operational blind spots, ethical drift, and systemic vulnerabilities before they escalate into crises. 

Financially, market actors, credit rating agencies, and institutional investors place a distinct premium on independent oversight. This heightened governance credibility strengthens market trust, effectively lowering the organisation’s cost of capital and elevating long-term market valuation. Beyond oversight, independent Directors act as confidential sounding Boards and mentors for the CEO, offering unbiased counsel during critical, high-stakes decisions. Furthermore, their extensive external networks unlock strategic partnerships, key industry access, and regulatory insights otherwise out of reach. Finally, a reputation for transparent, well-governed leadership serves as a powerful talent magnet, attracting elite executive leadership to the organisation.

Controlling shareholders may have mixed feelings. On the positive side, truly independent Directors boost credibility and lower the cost of capital, as institutional investors award governance premiums to strongly independent Boards. They also bring diverse industry experience, objective risk assessments, and fresh perspectives, helping founder-led firms navigate market disruptions and succession planning without internal bias. 

Conversely, controlling shareholders may fear losing strategic agility and control. Independent Directors are expected to scrutinise major capital investments and related-party deals, potentially slowing down decision-making. Additionally, because they lack day-to-day operational immersion, independent Directors can suffer from information asymmetry, leading to overly cautious governance that conflicts with founding shareholders’ bold vision. Ultimately, despite creating tension between executive control and external oversight, independent Directors remain indispensable for modern corporate governance.

FTX collapsed in 2022 when founder Sam Bankman-Fried operated without independent Board oversight, siphoning over $ 8 billion in customer funds into Alameda Research without risk controls or audits. WeWork cratered in 2019 before its aborted IPO because an obliging Board granted CEO Adam Neumann super-majority voting power, ignoring blatant self-dealing and unchecked spending. Both disasters prove that without independent Directors willing to exercise true oversight, unchecked power will inevitably burn the house to the ground.


Escaping such quiet traps requires truly progressive organisations to rethink Director sourcing strategies. Boards must look beyond traditional executive networks and build talent pools of active functional specialists and mid-career professionals motivated by professional impact rather than financial gain. Term limits and genuine peer evaluations must replace the automatic re-election of comfortable incumbents. Only by screening out passive income seekers can organisations ensure that Board seats remain in the hands of dedicated stewards truly driven to protect shareholders and guide the enterprise forward.

The true value of a Board member lies in thought independence, the intellectual autonomy, moral courage, and domain mastery required to serve as a dedicated fiduciary. To determine whether a candidate possesses this quality, nominating committees and institutional investors must look beyond compliance checklists and analyse behavioral evidence across his/her career. A candidate’s track record reveals critical traits that no regulatory questionnaire can capture.

 First among these is a demonstrated history of constructive dissent. True independence requires the willingness to take a lonely, unpopular stand when corporate integrity or strategy is at risk. Tangible records can reveal whether an individual has previously voted against management on critical issues such as executive compensation, risky acquisitions, or flawed succession plans, or resigned when governance standards were compromised. A history of principled dissent proves that a Director values duty above personal comfort or Board tenure.

Beyond moral courage, a candidate’s record reflects his/her analytical rigour. Psychological independence manifests as persistent curiosity and a refusal to accept management narratives at face value. A thorough evaluation shows whether a Director consistently asks probing questions about capital allocation, risk exposure, and operational execution; insists on independent external advice during complex transactions; and has the domain mastery to spot red flags before they escalate into systemic crises.

To recruit truly independent Directors, organisations must look beyond cosy referral networks and cast a wider net. Engaging specialised Board advisory firms eliminates internal bias, while skills-matrix benchmarking helps identify leaders with domain mastery in cybersecurity, ESG, and market expansion, and like. Using accredited pools of the Sri Lanka Institute of Directors (SLID) and maintaining open portals democratises sourcing, bringing fresh, uncompromised perspectives into the Boardroom. 

Yet, true independence is not merely a credential; it is a posture of courage. Professional bodies like SLID must cultivate Directors defined by character rather than compliance. By deploying psychometric screening to assess cognitive resilience, maintaining a vetted databank of certified visionaries, and enforcing continuous 360-degree reviews, SLID can breed a new generation of Board leaders. Through rigorous, management-independent training, it can equip these stewards with objective thought. A robust professional code can ensure they enter Boardrooms not to seek approval, but to safeguard integrity, challenge authority, and champion truth.


Let us ponder. When Independent Directors lose their courage, the light of accountability goes dark. A Boardroom is not meant to be a choir of agreement or a sanctuary for unchecked egos. It is the frontline defense of trust. When independent stewards bend their knees to charismatic founders, they trade truth for compliance, bury risk in silence, and let billions vanish into air. True governance requires the spine to stand, the willingness to ask the hard questions, and the unwavering conviction to protect those who placed their faith in the institution. An independent Board is the anchor that holds steady against the storm of greed, and without it, even the greatest titans will drift into ruin.

(The author is a Leadership Coach, Mentor and Consultant and boasts over 50+ years of experience in very senior positions in the corporate world – local and overseas. He can be reached at www.ronniepeiris.com)

title: Sri Lanka voted for ‘system change’. Two years on, the harder question is whether power itself has changed | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 9 October 2026 00:22
-     - 75

The NPP came to office promising more than another change of government. It promised to break with the habits of Sri Lankan power. Two years into Anura Kumara Dissanayake’s presidency, there are genuine reforms to show for that mandate but also uncomfortable evidence that some of the country’s oldest political patterns remain remarkably resilient

Sri Lankan politics has never lacked extravagant promises. Political folklore still remembers Sirimavo Bandaranaike’s 1970 campaign pledge to restore the second measure of the rice ration and the famous claim associated with that election that the rice would be found even if it had to be brought “from the moon”. Whether remembered today as rhetorical excess or an artefact of another political era, the story survived because it captured something more enduring about democratic politics: opposition is where governments imagine possibilities; office is where they discover constraints. 

The more consequential history, however, concerns promises about power itself. Chandrika Bandaranaike Kumaratunga entered the presidency in 1994 on an explicit reform mandate and vowed to abolish the executive presidency by July 1995. She pursued constitutional reform, but the presidency survived. Two decades later, Maithripala Sirisena won another mandate centred on democratic reform and curbing presidential authority. The 19th Amendment in 2015 did reduce presidential powers, restore independent commissions and reimpose a two-term limit, but parliament itself acknowledged that the executive presidency remained and that complete abolition would require further constitutional change. Between those two reform moments came Mahinda Rajapaksa’s 18th Amendment in 2010, which did something still more revealing about the attraction of executive authority: it removed the constitutional two-term limit on the presidency.

This is the political inheritance against which the National People’s Power must be judged. The NPP did not invent Sri Lanka’s habit of promising more outside government than can later be delivered from inside it. What distinguished the movement in 2024 was its insistence that it intended to break precisely that pattern.

When Anura Kumara Dissanayake entered the presidency on 23 September 2024, Sri Lanka was emerging from more than an economic catastrophe. Sovereign default, shortages and the upheaval of 2022 had become a broader crisis of political legitimacy, driven by the belief that patronage, impunity, concentrated executive authority and politically captured institutions had contributed to the country’s collapse. The NPP’s answer was not simply competent administration. It promised system change: constitutional reform, abolition of the executive presidency, stronger independent institutions, professional policing, anti-corruption enforcement, reduced political privilege and a state in which access to justice would not depend upon surname, ethnicity or proximity to government.

Sri Lankans responded by giving it exceptional democratic power. At the November 2024 parliamentary election the NPP won 159 of 225 seats, leaving its nearest rival with 40. In Jaffna district, hardly traditional JVP territory, it finished first with 80,830 votes, 24.85% of the total, and three seats. The significance of those numbers reaches beyond electoral arithmetic. A political movement whose organisational core, the Janatha Vimukthi Peramuna, had twice pursued revolutionary change through armed insurrection had been handed the state through a ballot box instead.

That should be understood as one of the most important democratic messages of 2024. Sri Lankan voters demonstrated that they did not need another revolution to dismantle an entrenched political establishment. They were prepared to hand even a movement with the JVP’s difficult history an opportunity to govern if it could persuade them that it offered a credible democratic alternative. The greater obligation created by that result was therefore never simply to complete a manifesto checklist; it was to justify the confidence that political transformation could occur through democratic institutions.

The oldest reform promise remains the hardest one

Nowhere is the tension between opposition principle and governing power clearer than in the executive presidency. The NPP explicitly campaigned on constitutional change and abolition of the executive presidential system. Yet two years into Dissanayake’s presidency, the institution remains intact, and in June 2026 Public Administration Minister Chandana Abayaratne acknowledged that abolition remained an election promise while saying it was “not a priority” for the government at that moment.

There are perfectly legitimate reasons not to rewrite a constitution according to an electoral stopwatch. Abolishing the presidency requires decisions about parliament, devolution, executive authority, electoral representation and the constitutional balance between institutions. Kumaratunga’s experience after 1994 and the partial reform achieved under Sirisena demonstrate that these difficulties are real. But they were not discovered after September 2024. They existed when the promise was made.

That history matters because abolition of the executive presidency has become almost a laboratory experiment in how Sri Lankan politicians behave around power. Governments repeatedly inherit an institution their predecessors condemned; reform becomes more complicated once its powers are available to the new occupant. The NPP claimed that it represented a break with this cycle, which means its obligation is greater than explaining why constitutional reform is difficult. It must eventually demonstrate whether an institution diagnosed as a structural problem while the movement was outside government remains a structural problem once the movement controls it.

This is not to say the NPP has done nothing. That would be contradicted by the record. Parliament enacted the Proceeds of Crime Act in April 2025, introduced new asset-and-liability declaration regulations, amended the National Audit Act, and in September 2025 repealed the statutory entitlement regime for former presidents. The latter reform abolished residences, monthly allowances, secretarial allowances, official transport and several other benefits previously provided under law to former presidents and their widows. These are tangible changes and should be counted as such.

But they also illuminate the distinction at the centre of the NPP’s first two years. Removing privileges from former holders of power is easier than surrendering powers available to the current holder. Passing accountability legislation is important; proving that accountability institutions can act independently when their work becomes politically inconvenient is harder. The smaller achievements cannot indefinitely substitute for the larger reforms from which the promise of system change derived much of its force.

Minority trust was won. Justice remains a much larger task

The NPP also deserves to be assessed differently from governments that built electoral legitimacy explicitly through ethnic majoritarianism. Its 2024 parliamentary breakthrough in Jaffna was evidence that at least a significant section of Tamil voters was prepared to test a national movement historically associated with Sinhala-majority southern politics. That was politically important in a country whose post-independence history has repeatedly demonstrated how difficult it is for national parties to acquire genuine confidence across ethnic divisions.

It would therefore be inaccurate to describe the NPP government as simply indifferent to minority concerns. Official figures say 615 acres of land had been released since the government took office through June 2026, on top of 9,480 acres released between the end of the war and December 2024. Nor has the government ignored the enormous unresolved caseload concerning the disappeared. Cabinet disclosed in September 2025 that the Office on Missing Persons had received 16,966 complaints, of which 10,517 remained pending investigation, and approved a special project intended to complete those investigations and related work by the end of 2027.

Those figures demonstrate both action and the scale of what remains. More than 10,000 unresolved complaints are not merely an administrative backlog. They represent families who have lived for years, and in many cases decades, without answers. Releasing land is meaningful, but it is not equivalent to resolving the deeper questions of disappearance, accountability, devolution and political representation that continue to shape relations between the state and communities in the north and east.

Human Rights Watch’s 2026 assessment was particularly critical, arguing that despite the government’s rhetoric of national reconciliation it had done too little to build confidence among Tamil and Muslim communities, while several promised legal reforms remained incomplete. That is an advocacy organisation’s assessment rather than an uncontested verdict, but it underscores a distinction the government cannot avoid: being less reliant on ethnonationalist politics than some predecessors is not itself the same as delivering justice.

Minority voters gave the NPP something difficult to obtain and easy to lose trust in the possibility that national politics could operate differently. The historical significance of that opportunity should make delivery, rather than rhetoric, the standard by which it is judged.

Judicial independence and the problem of unnecessary doubt

The same standard should apply to the judiciary. At a May Day rally in 2026, Dissanayake referred to a judicial decision due later that month and indicated that supporters would have reason to applaud when it was delivered. The Bar Association of Sri Lanka responded with “grave concern”, saying the tenor of the remarks was open to the suggestion of interference and could erode public confidence in the judiciary.

The limits of what can responsibly be claimed here are important. There is no evidence that the president privately communicated with the judges, knew the judgment in advance or determined its outcome. Those would be much more serious allegations and should not be inferred without evidence. But a government elected on a programme of depoliticisation should understand why even the perception of executive expectation around a pending judgment is damaging. Judicial independence depends not merely upon politicians refraining from issuing direct orders to judges; it depends upon maintaining sufficient institutional distance that judgments for the government do not appear compliant and judgments against it do not appear defiant.

That point becomes especially important when accountability is directed at members of previous administrations. There is nothing inherently suspicious about investigating former presidents, Rajapaksas or opposition politicians. If credible evidence exists, failing to investigate them because they are politically powerful would reproduce precisely the impunity Sri Lanka was promised would end.

Yet prosecutions of yesterday’s rulers cannot themselves establish that the system has become impartial. The real test arrives when credible allegations concern an NPP minister, JVP official, senior government appointee or political ally. The question then will be whether investigators move with the same urgency, prosecutors apply the same evidentiary thresholds and ministers protect the institution rather than the individual. That principle was already at the centre of the original argument: justice becomes credible when it can move inward as readily as outward.

The PTA is a reminder that states surrender coercive power reluctantly

The Prevention of Terrorism Act presents an even sharper test. The NPP campaigned on abolishing oppressive legislation including the PTA, yet the government disclosed that 49 people were arrested under it in the first five months of 2025, compared with 38 during all of 2024. Amnesty International recorded the continued use of the legislation, including beyond conventional terrorism cases.

The case of Mohamad Liyaudeen Mohamed Rusdi illustrates why that matters. He was arrested by the Counter Terrorism and Investigation Division in March 2025, with allegations including his display of two anti-Israel stickers. Dissanayake, acting as defence minister, issued a detention order. After examining the evidence, the Human Rights Commission found insufficient material establishing an offence under the PTA, and Rusdi was released in April. The Commission said investigators had acknowledged that the words on the stickers did not themselves constitute a PTA offence.

The government subsequently drafted replacement counter-terrorism legislation, but Human Rights Watch argued in January 2026 that significant provisions risked reproducing powers associated with the PTA, including broad definitions and extensive detention authority. Again, that is the assessment of a rights organisation, not a court ruling. But it raises a question that lies at the heart of system change: does reform mean trusting a new government to use inherited coercive powers more responsibly, or designing institutions so that no government can easily abuse them?

For the JVP, this should be more than an abstract constitutional debate. Its own history demonstrates what can happen when coercive state power is exercised without sufficient restraint. A movement that once suffered brutal repression by the state now possesses authority over that state; few political movements have had a clearer historical reason to understand why safeguards must survive the goodwill of the people temporarily in charge.

Recovery is measurable. So is the hardship that remains

The government’s economic record also requires more nuance than either celebration or dismissal. Sri Lanka’s recovery is real. The World Bank recorded 5% economic growth in 2024, while the IMF reported this week that output expanded 4.2% year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026, marking an 11th consecutive quarter of growth. Maintaining the IMF-supported stabilisation framework, despite the JVP’s history and earlier criticism of parts of that programme, has also demonstrated a pragmatic willingness to govern within constraints that campaign politics can sometimes obscure.

But the social legacy of the crisis remains severe. The World Bank estimated poverty at 24.5% in 2024, around twice the 2019 level; food prices had more than doubled between 2021 and 2024, employment remained weak and real wages were still below their 2019 levels. By October 2025 the Bank was still describing the recovery as “uneven and incomplete”, noting that national output remained below its 2018 level.

No serious analysis should attribute that hardship entirely to a government that inherited the aftermath of collapse. But the statistics matter because the NPP promised more than macroeconomic stabilisation. Its political challenge is to demonstrate that stability eventually reaches households with higher incomes, better employment, functioning public services and economic security. An economy can recover in aggregate long before citizens experience recovery in their own lives.

The real promise was not 1,325 promises

This is why reducing the NPP’s first two years to a percentage of manifesto commitments misses the larger story. Sri Lanka has experienced generations of governments that promised more than they delivered. The rice-ration politics of the 1970s belonged to one era; repeated promises to abolish the executive presidency belonged to another. The recurring problem has been less that politicians make promises  all democracies produce than that the behaviour of power repeatedly proves more durable than the movements that promised to reform it.

The NPP’s democratic achievement in 2024 was substantial. It displaced much of the established political order without violence, won support well beyond the JVP’s historical base and obtained 159 parliamentary seats through an election. It has since enacted meaningful anti-corruption and governance measures and preserved a difficult economic stabilisation. These are not illusions and should not be described as such.

But neither should they obscure what remains unresolved. The executive presidency the NPP pledged to abolish survives, with abolition no longer an immediate priority. More than 10,000 complaints before the Office on Missing Persons remained pending when the government approved its latest program. The PTA was used dozens of times after the NPP entered office, and its proposed replacement has attracted serious human-rights criticism. A presidential remark concerning a pending judgment prompted the Bar Association to warn about public confidence in judicial independence. The economic recovery is measurable, but so is poverty at roughly twice its pre-crisis level.

None of this establishes that the NPP has become indistinguishable from the governments it defeated, and two years is too short a period for such a sweeping conclusion. It does establish something more useful: the distance between changing the people who control a political system and changing the incentives, powers and institutions through which that system operates.

The most important message of 2024 may ultimately be directed not at Sri Lanka’s old political establishment but at the JVP itself. The movement once believed revolutionary change required confrontation with the state. Decades later, Sri Lankan voters demonstrated something more democratic and more powerful: if a political movement gives them sufficient reason to trust it, they are prepared to hand it to the state peacefully.

That trust carries an obligation greater than fulfilling every campaign pledge. It requires proving that governments do not inevitably become prisoners of the powers they once promised to restrain. Two years into the NPP experiment, that question remains open and it may matter far more to Sri Lanka’s democratic future than whether any government can ever promise to bring rice from the moon.

(The author is an International Relations student at Monash University whose writing explores politics, governance, and international affairs)

title: Killing the golden goose –  Sri Lanka’s solar energy fiasco | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 9 October 2026 00:20
-     - 141

The Government’s decision to scrap two of the three schemes which allow rooftop solar energy systems to connect to the national electricity grid has caused shock waves and weakened new installation demand.
Before deciding whether that change is justified, it is worth understanding how rooftop solar became so important — and what it now does to the electricity system. 

The Public Utilities Commission of Sri Lanka (PUCSL) reports that rooftop solar reached 2,472 MW of installed capacity by 31 December 2025: 2,120 MW connected through CEB and 352 MW through LECO. Using PUCSL’s consumer rule of thumb of 115–120 kWh of monthly generation for each installed kW, a mature 2.5 GW rooftop fleet would produce roughly 3,450–3,600 GWh a year, or about 9.5–10.0 GWh on an average day. (This is a run-rate estimate, not reported 2025 generation: PUCSL records 1,938 GWh of rooftop generation in 2025 while capacity was still growing rapidly during the year.)

How rooftop solar took off

Rooftop solar now makes up 19.4% of Sri Lanka’s total electricity generation. In other words, one fifth of our electricity now comes from solar power on people’s roofs, a clean, renewable source of energy with no capital cost burden on the Government. This is also 56% or just over half of our annual hydroelectricity generation of 6,306GWh as reported by PUCSL for the year 2025.

The Government facilitated solar roofs by allowing “net metering” which allows the electricity utilities, CEB (Now called NSO-National System Operator) and LECO customers to set off electricity exported against electricity imported, paying only the difference if there is a deficit and receiving an “electricity credit” if export is more than import. Net metering became Government policy thanks to the efforts of a few dedicated individuals including the late Herath Dissanayake who sadly passed away last month. This scheme was further expanded to include “net accounting” where any exported electricity after the electricity “set off” received a payment from the utility and “net plus” which kept export and import separate, paying for imported electricity while obtaining payment for export. The initial rate for electricity payment also called the “feed in tariff” was calculated on an ad hoc basis and later by a comprehensive formula developed later by the electric utility’s own whiz kids. Despite initial objection, this formula was accepted as a fair solution for the feed in tariff calculation. The fair and transparent feed in tariff, increasing electricity prices, falling solar module and inverter prices, became the formula for rapid expansion. Sri Lanka’s own entrepreneurs stepped in utilising decades of human seed capital from a massively successful rural solar program of the last decade. Finally the nearly unlimited financial resources of our wholesale importers also joined in, and the industry mushroomed creating nearly a thousand small solar companies and tens of thousands of foot soldiers, for sales and installation work. The big names too joined the fray bringing their access to capital, distribution channels and name brands to bear. Retail banks joined in with an Asian Development Bank(ADB) refinance scheme. The result was massive capacity increase and growth of the industry. The industry associations claim that the industry has 1000 active solar companies with 40,000 are direct employees.

Two events that changed the debate

Monkey business – The February 2025 blackout

On a sunny Sunday in February 2025, the entire national electricity grid went down and it took much of the day to restore. Naturally everyone looked for a culprit and initially the monkey that apparently caused the short circuit was blamed. Then the blame shifted to rooftop solar. The theory that took hold was that there was simply too much solar on the grid and that rooftop solar had made the system unstable. This has subsequently become one of the arguments used to justify curtailing rooftop solar. But what actually happened is much more interesting.

The fault occurred at the Panadura grid substation at around 11.13 a.m. It was a sunny Sunday; electricity demand was low and rooftop solar was supplying a very large part of daytime demand. This meant that the national grid was seeing only the balance of the electricity being consumed in homes and businesses, after their rooftop solar generation had been deducted. When the Panadura fault occurred, voltage in the surrounding network dropped sharply and a quantity of rooftop and other embedded solar automatically disconnected to protect itself. The fault itself was cleared very quickly and system voltage recovered to normal in about one second. The problem was that the solar which had disconnected did not come back with it. 


A simple example explains what happened. Imagine an area consuming 100 MW of electricity but producing 60 MW from rooftop solar. The national grid only has to supply the remaining 40 MW. If a disturbance causes that 60 MW of solar disconnect, when the voltage recovers the consumers still require their 100 MW, but the solar is no longer there. The national grid which was supplying 40 MW suddenly must find 100 MW. This is not just theory. Measurements following the Panadura fault showed that power flowing into the affected area increased by about 25 MW after the fault was cleared, consistent with embedded solar generation having disconnected.

Rooftop solar inverters were required to wait 60 seconds before reconnecting to the grid. The grid therefore recovered almost immediately, while the solar generation it had been relying on remained absent for at least another minute.

The effect was immediate. Electricity which only moments earlier had been supplied locally by rooftop solar now had to come from the national grid. Measurements on the transmission lines serving the affected area showed power flowing into it increasing by about 25 MW after the fault was cleared. But this was only what could be observed on those particular transmission lines. It does not tell us how much solar generation may have disconnected across the wider Western Province, where rooftop solar is heavily concentrated, or elsewhere in the country.

The system was therefore suddenly faced with a very different balance between supply and demand. Conventional generators had to pick up electricity which, seconds earlier, had been supplied by solar. Frequency began to fall. As it fell, more solar inverters elsewhere disconnected on their protection settings. Each additional loss of solar increased the amount of electricity the conventional generators had to supply, pushing frequency still lower. What began as a local electrical fault was becoming a national problem.

The automatic load-shedding system then operated, but here another consequence of the growth of rooftop solar became apparent. The system had been designed for an electricity network in which switching off a distribution feeder removed roughly the amount of consumer demand carried by that feeder. That was no longer necessarily true. By 2025 many feeders contained substantial rooftop generation as well as consumption. Disconnecting such a feeder therefore removed both the remaining demand on the national grid and the solar generation embedded within it. The actual relief to the grid could consequently be much smaller than expected.

The downward spiral continued. At 11:13:58 New Laxapana tripped on under-frequency protection. Within milliseconds Samanalawewa, Old Laxapana, Uma Oya and Victoria followed. Shortly afterwards the three operating units at Norochcholai also tripped. Less than half a minute after the original fault at Panadura, the national grid had collapsed.

The important point is that rooftop solar did play a part in the blackout, however it did not cause it nor is it fair to say that we have too much solar and it had made the grid unstable. It’s true that a large amount of solar is now operating on the grid, the monitoring, protection and operating arrangements have not kept pace with it.

The Engineers’ plus, plus

The second event of significance to the industry was a new scheme launched in 2024 by the utility companies, called “net plus plus”. The origin of this scheme remains a mystery as the industry never requested it and it is suspected that a group of engineers within the electricity utility itself created it. This scheme completely removed the link between the customers’ contract demand and the size of the rooftop solar system they could install. (30A single phase - 5 kW, 60A three phase - 20 kW, 60A three phase – 40 kW) Under the net plus plus scheme all that was needed was the area engineer’s approval to install the largest 40 kW system even on the smallest house.

The scheme also separated the utility customer/roof owner from the actual developer, allowing investors to take advantage of someone else’s roof space anywhere in the country to install a system, in fact even roof space was not a limiting factor with massive solar arrays being installed on tiny roofs became a common sight.

This scheme became a windfall for many “investors”. 

At the peak Rs.37/kWh feed-in tariff, a 40-kW system producing about 5,000 kWh a month would earn roughly Rs.185,000 a month. On an investment of about Rs.4.5 million, the simple first-year cash yield is about 49%, with a simple payback of just over two years before allowing for degradation, maintenance and inverter replacement. The fast-growing solar industry accelerated even further as opportunistic investors rushed to benefit from this windfall scheme. Finally, when it dawned on the authorities that the scheme was being abused, it was suddenly scrapped.

The bigger picture

So why did the Government scrap “net metering” and “net accounting” schemes leaving only the “net plus” scheme which makes customers buy electricity from the utilities at a high price while selling the solar electricity at a lower price. A scheme that makes no economic sense to a household. 

The Government claims that around 85,000–90,000 rooftop solar customers under Net Accounting are benefiting financially at the expense of around 7 million electricity consumers.

In other words, the Government is saying that we lose money buying electricity from solar roofs during the day while supplying high-cost thermally generated electricity at night when solar is not available.

Is this correct?

The assumption that solar generation during the day is more expensive to the Government is fundamentally flawed. The now significant rooftop solar generation of around 9.7Gwh per day has effectively pushed the daytime hydro generation to the nighttime minimising thermal generation use. (see table and graph below)

Sri Lanka: Shift of major hydro to the evening peak

March 2020–2025 dispatch comparison and March 2025 hydro-battery headroom

Method: average 15-minute Major Hydro dispatch for comparable weekdays during 1–17 March of each year. Midday is 10:00–15:00 and evening is 18:30–22:30. The 2025 sample is limited to the PUCSL March data available through 17 March.

Figure 1. Average major-hydro output on comparable March weekdays.

What the shift shows

The evening-to-midday hydro ratio rose from about 1.3× in 2020–21 to 1.85× in 2024 and 2.57× in early March 2025. This is consistent with reservoir hydro being backed down during solar hours and conserved for the evening ramp. The timing coincides with rapid rooftop-solar growth, although rainfall, reservoir conditions, demand and thermal-plant availability also affect hydro dispatch.

PUCSL Daily Solar and Hydro Generation - 18 March 2025

The PUCSL daily report provides a useful visual cross-check of the dispatch analysis. On 18 March, major hydro falls to roughly 150-200 MW around the middle of the day, then rises sharply as solar output declines, reaching roughly 1,100 MW around the evening peak. The solar chart shown by PUCSL is based on telemetered solar stations only; it therefore does not show the much larger behind-the-meter rooftop-solar contribution.

This is a tremendous windfall for the NSO and the country which should use this information to recalculate its actual cost of nighttime generation. This phenomenon is in effect like the pump storage systems adopted by many countries to store solar energy by pumping water back into reservoirs to use at night.
